Mr. Speaker, first I would like to commend the hon. member for introducing the motion. This is one of the few opportunities we have to say something in this House about the service we have been getting from a Crown agency called the Post Office. My city of Mississauga has the privilege of having the largest postal warehouse in all of Canada. Indeed, the statement around my riding is that the reason we pay 17 cents is that ten cents is to finance storage at Gateway and 7 cents is for delivery.
People throughout Canada-I am sure this applies in your riding, Mr. Speaker, as it does in the parliamentary secretary's riding-are very disturbed about the inadequate, incompetent and inept service they receive from their Post Office. It bothers me that hard-working individuals who work for our Post Office are afraid to tell their neighbours that they are employees of the Post Office Department because of the reputation of that organization.
Studies have indicated clearly that the management of the Post Office is probably the worst management of any organization, not just of this size but of almost any organization in the whole of the country. It should be impossible for the parliamentary secretary, who just finished speaking, to say, as she did, that things are improving in Calgary or in western Canada, perhaps, and to apologize for the lack of Saturday delivery.
We want delivery, and the fact that post offices are not open on Saturday as they used to be, and the fact that we do not get
July 7, 1980

delivery twice a day as we used to get, are not the real issue. The issue is that we want delivery, period. Hon. members of this House find that their mail takes seven to ten days to be delivered. They send out householders, as I did in March, only to find that they are delivered in late April. Individual citizens throughout Canada continue to call us and complain about lack of service, delay in service, missing deliveries, and destroyed packages. When we have all these complaints, there is something serious.
My constituency office in Mississauga receives its stationery and other material for distribution through the use of the Post Office. These materials are delivered to my constituency office from Ottawa. Frequently the material is put into a mail bag and delivered to my office in the mail bag. What happens is that a good part of the stationery arrives completely destroyed, to the point that my executive assistant in my constituency office the other day telephoned our local postmaster and said, "I am very pleased to hear that you have a new elephant." He was abashed and asked, "What do you mean a new elephant? We do not have an elephant at all". My executive assistant said, "You must have an elephant; how else could you possibly destroy five boxes of new stationery?" There is something wrong here, and the hon. member's motion allowing this debate in the House today is very appropriate.
Hardly a day goes by when hon. members or their constituency offices do not have to listen to the complaints of constituents concerning the mail, to the point that one just throws up his hands and says, "Well, that is the way it is; something must be done." Business, hon. members of this House and, indeed, government departments here refuse to use the postal service. If they really want something delivered they call upon Air Canada or Purolator, but they do not call on the Post Office because they know that this organization which we support to the extent of well in excess of $400 million a year, over and above postal charges, is not competent to ensure delivery of any article to anywhere from anywhere. That is a pretty disturbing thing.
There has to be a better way, and some better ways are available. Let me say this to members of the Post Office through you, sir, that there is such a thing as an electronic transfer of funds, there is such a thing as transmitting messages by wire, by radio, by cable, and by video. There have been studies done by this government with regard to the transfer of pension cheques, of payroll cheques and all other transmissions which this government does, ranging from family allowances to pension cheques, to the bank accounts of individuals by electronic transfer. That very program would save some 60,000 jobs in the public service. That very program would ensure the delivery of pension cheques. It would ensure that John Brown, who never received his war veterans allowance last week, would have it on June 30 in his bank account where it belongs, and would not have to call his member of Parliament or the pension office to find out what happened to it.
Postal Service
This situation has gone on for long enough. If members working in the Post Office, if management in the Post Office, and if the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) himself cannot get his act together and provide the kind of service that we Canadians used to enjoy and should still enjoy, then other methods of transmitting information by the government transferring funds and by business transferring funds, will have to be employed. There are other methods, which might be somewhat costly, but the way things are going the Post Office should get its act together very quickly or it need not exist in this country.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF RESTORING ADEQUATE LEVELS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to address myself to the motion of the hon. member with regard to the Post Office. He used the phrases "restoring adequate levels of postal service" and "no further cutbacks in postal service" in a manner which would have us believe that service levels at the Post Office are woefully inadequate. That is an assumption which is not borne out by facts. May I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the meaning of the hon. member's motion. He used the phrase "restoring adequate levels of postal service" as if there had existed in the past a veritable golden age in the mails. This attitude reflects a complete disregard for present day realities. It reflects a mentality which does not examine facts.
The hon. member talks of "restoring adequate levels of postal service". The facts of the matter are that never before in its long and distinguished history has Canada Post provided such a high level of performance and reliability in the mails as it does today. The hon. member says "restore adequate levels of service". I submit that the word "restore" signifies to go back and do over again. To what period in Canadian history would the hon. member have the Post Office return-to the age of the horse when relays of ponies galloped between towns carrying the mail bags? Or perhaps he would have the Post Office go back to the age of steam when the great iron horses first thundered across this great country carrying messages that would link and bind it together?
I am not suggesting that, in its long history of contributing to the social, political, artistic and commercial fabric of the nation, the Post Office was not well served by the horse, train and truck, not at all. The Post Office always has availed itself of the best technology of the day. That is its tradition, a tradition of adapting to change and exploiting new and better ways of doing things.
I sketched this brief history of the mails to put the Post Office in perspective. It is in the best interests of us all that we look at the operation of the mails objectively, without sentiment, and without lamenting the past, as the hon. member has done, or of conceiving extravagant hopes for the future. Unless we bring a balanced perspective in examining the Post Office, we will lose sight of what we can do to improve it and what we cannot do. The fact of the matters is that the Post Office has now entered the satellite and electronic age. It has become modern. We cannot, as the hon. member suggests, "go back and restore".

Postal Service
In the interests of time I should like to refer to an episode with regard to Canada Post to which originally I wanted to refer toward the end of my intervention, and which I do not want to omit. I want to focus on this episode at Canada Post which I believe illustrates clearly its performance and the performance to which Canadians have become accustomed. Only a few weeks ago several thousands of the more than two and one quarter million family allowance cheques which the government sends out monthly did not arrive on the appointed day in a number of communities in Ontario. Immediately there was a public outcry over the delay. Let me hasten to add that the outcry began before the delay was one day old. Such is the Post Office's performance that the public has, over a sustained period of time, come to expect that family allowance cheques arrive on time as a matter of course. I think these high expectations reflect an extremely efficient postal service.
The family allowance episode illustrates another phenomenon about the Post Office, that is, that as we get still better we can expect still more criticism. This might seem like a paradox, but it is not. It is a matter of higher expectations. Shortcomings in the mails which were tolerated patiently in the past as being inevitable, seem unendurable as soon as the idea of solving them crosses people's minds. All the shortcomings then removed call attention to those that remain, and now they appear more galling. The shortcomings, it is true, have been reduced, but sensibility to them has become more acute. A generation ago, before the advent of the jet aeroplane, a one day delay of the cheques in the mail would have passed unnoticed. That is not the case today. We live in an era dominated by electronics and the computer. The public have come to expect the same almost semi-automatic results in the mails that they get from electronic gadgetry and from the computers. This is impossible in such a labour-intensive business as the Post Office. Nevertheles, our Canada Post levels of service compare favourably with any post office in the western world.
I do not lament the past as does the hon. member who would, as I said in my introduction, "restore" the post office. I do not share any such romantic notions about returning to the days of steam and the horse. I am, however, inspired by the recent achievements of Canada Post. These achievements inspire our staff to provide Canadians with a postal service second to none. The Post Office is not restoring, it is advancing. Let me tell you about a few of these advances.
In 1948 intercity mail went to air. That is, all first class mail went air mail. We were one of the first countries in the world to enter the air age totally and completely. Now, of course, all innovations are not without some shortcomings. At times fog over St. John's or a whiteout over Inuvik would prevent the aeroplane carrying the mail from landing, sometimes for a day or two. But is that an argument for going back to the horse and buggy?
In reviewing where the Post Office has been and where it is headed, I would remind the hon. member that we no longer
July 7, 1980
live in a letter writing age. It would be inconceivable for our age to produce a Voltaire whose letters in the Besterman edition come to more than 100 volumes.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pepin that Bill S-6, to amend the Two-Price Wheat Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before five o'clock I mentioned the fact that it has been a long time-as a matter of fact it has been seven years-since the price of wheat could be discussed in the House of Commons. This bill was introduced by the previous Liberal administration and called Bill C-24, once under the legislation of the Progressive Conservative government called Bill C-7, and we have it here in the form of a Senate bill, Bill S-6. It is interesting that it has taken over two years for this bill to come on the floor of the House, to deal with something that is as important to the producers of western Canada as what they receive per bushel for grain.
1 should like to answer a few questions in my own mind as to why this bill is here. Is it for the wheat producers of western Canada? Is it for the consumer? I do not think it is for either of those groups. It is to remove the liability of the present Liberal government to the tune of $200 million which it owes the farmers of western Canada and which will legally become due before July 31 of this year. This is a lot of money. We are talking about a drought in western Canada. There was a lot of hullabaloo and a lot of hoopla as to a possible $60 million pay-out to the producers of western Canada, in the cattle business, because of the drought. Here we have a bill by which this government is attempting to remove its legal obligation to the tune of some $200 million, three times what it is purport-
July 7, 1980

ing to give the cattlemen and wheat producers of western Canada.
When the Two-Price Wheat Act was first introduced in the House in 1974 by Otto Lang, he said the following:
This is a bill whose specific purpose is to enshrine for a period of years, in this ase for seven years, a procedure whereby the treasury supplements payments made for wheat designed for human consumption in Canada-
It is in its present form without any doubt and, I should think without any argument, in the nature of a consumer subsidy, an amount paid by the treasury, on behalf of the people of Canada as taxpayers, to lighten the burden on the consumer of the cost of wheat products in Canada.
Those were the comments of Otto Lang when it was introduced for second reading on October 29, 1974.
What happened with the introduction of that bill was that the wheat producers or the farmers of western Canada had the price of their wheat frozen for seven years. It was seven years that this bill was to run. I do not know of any other contract with longshoremen, Post Office workers or any other labour group, which goes for a term of seven years.

They may not run that long if things continue. But what happened with this bill is that the prices the farmers of western Canada were to receive from 1974 onwards were frozen. We felt at that time that it was unjust and we feel at this time that it is unjust, particularly when not carrying through on the commitment of seven years.
In the fall of 1978 the Liberal government of that day decided to terminate the subsidy payment to the producers in western Canada. Instead of a fixed domestic price and a subsidy payment, the regulations of the Canadian Wheat Board were used, setting the price farmers would receive for grain consumed domestically. At that time it was set at a price of $4 per bushel as the floor, and $5 per bushel at the upper end. That was the price in respect of spring wheat. In the case of Durum the regulations set the price at a floor of $4 per bushel up to $7.50. We cannot understand the difference in treatment in respect of Durum and spring wheat; we could not at the time and we can not now.
Without Bill S-6, to advance the termination date of November 30, 1978, instead of the end of July, 1980, which obligated this government to pay the producer what he has been receiving since December 1, 1978, directly from the marketplace, and without this retroactive termination of this bill, the government would in effect owe the farmers of western Canada $200 million.
Let us discuss, as we were doing at the beginning, whether this was a subsidy to the farmers of western Canada or a subsidy to the consumers of Canada. The transfer of income under the two-price wheat program from 1969 to 1978 amounted to $396 million from the taxpayer to the consumer, but from the taxpayer to the producer it amounted to $75 million, from the consumer to the producer it represented $40 million, and from the producer to the consumer it represented
Two-Price Wheat Act
an additional $35 million. Just using those numbers, $150 million was received by the producers, but $396 million was received by the consumers of Canada.
In addition, in the first four months of the 1979-80 crop year producers have subsidized the consumers another estimated $22 million. Furthermore, since the summer of 1979 producers have subsidized consumers up to $1 million a week.
This bill as introduced in 1974, and as we are discussing it today, is not subsidy to the farmers of western Canada, it is subsidy to the consumers of Canada. The cost of production is what a farmer is concerned about. If it cost him "x" to produce a bushel of grain and if he could make "x" plus, he considers that a profit, as any businessman would.
This government in 1974 refused to include indexing provisions for the cost of production in this bill. When the legislation was brought in, the price of wheat was around $6 a bushel. Today the price of wheat in Vancouver is $6.73 a bushel. It is strange how things go back. Durum today in Thunder Bay, or 1 should say at Vancouver, sells for $8.14 a bushel. Right now the farmer in Canada is receiving $5 a bushel for spring wheat consumed in Canada. If he were exporting it he would be exporting it at $6.73 per bushel.
"With levels which are still to this day pretty well close to record, we decided we should look at the proposition as between the Canadian Wheat Board on the one hand, other producers of wheat in Canada, and the consumers of Canada as represented by the buyers, millers and users. We decided we should enter into an arrangement whereby there would be a range of prices for grain; for wheat used for human consumption with a range that reflected more adequately than anything before the cost of production to consumers." That was said by Otto Lang in 1974. There has not been anything done to rectify the provision in this bill which does not recognize that the cost of production is what the farmer is concerned about. If he is going to sell wheat in Canada at a set price, a price set for a seven-year term, surely there should be some provision that, as times changed, he would be compensated for the increase in the cost of production.
The special adviser to the minister of state responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, the senator in waiting and twice defeated candidate for Assiniboia, at that time said:
-it has been argued that this legislation should reflect specifically costs of production. 1 think that kind of suggestion is somewhat inappropriate in a discussion on a two-price wheat system for wheat.
I would certainly hope that gentleman has changed his mind today, seven years later. It is very appropriate that the cost of production be considered in any pricing arrangement which ties people to a contract over a period of time as this measure tied the farmers for seven years.
In 1974 the member for Assiniboia at that time said:
-if conditions change drastically, as well they may, between now and 1980, if there is a downturn in the grain market-as grain producers of western Canada realize might happen-the figure provided for in the bill can be changed by this House to keep it in line with real circumstances.
At no time since this bill was passed in 1974 have members of Parliament had the opportunity to discuss the price of wheat

for domestic consumption. Even now there is no consultation between the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board and the government.
I would like briefly to refer to Senate Debates, May 29, where the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Argue) said he had made inquiries and had been informed that the advisory committee was not asked in any formal way to pass judgment on or to state its opinion about this policy. That is really not what the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board should be used for. That advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board is a duly elected body to represent the producers of western Canada and to advise the Wheat Board as to its feelings on government legislation affecting farmers.
Asked why the government had not considered any steps to go back to at least this crop year or the last half of this crop year in order to supply the farmers of western Canada with an adequate income by removing the $5 ceiling per bushel of wheat consumed domestically, the minister of state said he did not consider that a question the government was then considering, or in fact should be considering, because it would be setting forth policy and would obviously be something of a risk to producers. It certainly would be something of a risk to producers. The minister went on to say that to have a fixed price is a benefit to producers and is also a benefit to consumers. I really do not know how it is a benefit, when we look at history over the last seven years, to the grain producers of western Canada.
I should like to draw the attention of members to the price that will be paid into the Wheat Board's fund at any given time by Canadian millers, which is at the export price for 13'/2 per cent protein wheat, so that wheat producers can look forward in the next two years to a price for wheat sold to millers for domestic consumption ranging between $5 and $7 a bushel. That has reference to the new price for wheat consumed in Canada. The farmers in western Canada will receive between $5 and $7 a bushel.
Earlier I stated that right now in Vancouver wheat is selling for $6.73 per bushel. We have not reached the end of this crop year and the start of the next crop year, when this agreement is to come into effect, and already we are within 27 cents of being at the limit, so that the consumers will be subsidized once again by the producers of Canada for their consumption of grain.
I mentioned the 13.5 per cent protein level. Something very strange has happened with regard to protein. The elevator companies said that it was too difficult for them to put in place protein testers which would allow them to buy and sell grain at a protein level, that it was very expensive and something which they could not afford. It may be too expensive for the elevator companies, but the producers of western Canada have been asked to supply $1.5 million. They have been asked to supply
this money through a check-off of 75 cents a ton, in order that the elevator companies can buy this testing equipment.
At the same time the producers are being asked to pay 75 cents a ton to supply this testing equipment for the elevator companies, there is no provision anywhere in the legislation or in the grading system of the Canadian Grain Commission which says that farmers will be compensated for protein. In the next crop year there is no compensation provided to the farmers of western Canada for additional protein. During the similar debate in 1974 members on the opposition side warned the government that they should include an indexing provision for the cost of production or, as an alternative, that it shorten the seven years for which the farmers would be tied in.

On October 29, 1974, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), said, as it is quoted in Hansard at page 865:
-this bill lacks an effective measure to take into consideration the increased costs of production. Therefore we would recommend to the minister the implementation of such a provision to reflect the rising costs of production over the seven-year period.
It seems strange to those of us in western Canada that there are two products which are sold at below world price levels on the domestic market. Both those products come from western Canada. One of the products is wheat, and it is sold at less than the export price to the consumers in Canada. Of course the other commodity is oil. We in the west find that very strange. I am sure that if most of the people-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill S-l which in effect repeals the Two-Price Wheat Act on July 31, 1980, or an earlier date to be fixed by declaration-

speechtext: Bill S-6.

speechtext:
Or, on a retroactive basis, to amend the act, specifically section 3 thereof, which reduces the term of the bill from a period of July 1, 1974 to June 30, 1980, of July 1, 1974, to November 30, 1978 as it relates to the designated area within the Wheat Board.
The two-price wheat system was introduced in 1974 by the then minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, the Hon. Otto Lang. In the debate on the bill on October 29, 1974, the minister said, as reported at page 863 of Hansard:
This is a bill whose specific purpose is to enshrine for a period of years, in this case for seven years, a procedure whereby the treasury supplements payments made for wheat designed for human consumption in Canada.
And further down the same page there appears this statement:
It is in its present form without any doubt and, 1 should think without any argument, in the nature of a consumer subsidy, an amount paid by the treasury, on behalf of the people of Canada as taxpayers, to lighten the burden on the consumer of the cost of wheat products in Canada.
I should like to emphasize the words "seven years" and the words "the nature of a consumer subsidy". In effect, the bill placed a ceiling price on Red Spring wheat of $5 per bushel for domestic consumption, and at the same time it fixed the floor price for the same wheat at $3.25 per bushel. In the case of Durum wheat the ceiling price was $7.50 per bushel and the
floor price was $5.75. In other words, the millers and consum ers of domestic grain were able to purchase Red Spring whea and Durum wheat at the floor price, and the treasury-whic' in effect is the taxpayers of Canada-paid to the Canadia Wheat Board on behalf of the consumer, a subsidy which wa the difference between the floor price and the world wheat price, up to a maximum of $1.75 per bushel.
I should like to make it perfectly clear to members of th House that the $1.75 per bushel was not a subsidy to the grain producer because he was asked, indeed, forced to sell on the domestic market at less than he could sell at on the world market. He was simply paid the difference by the treasury up to a maximum of $1.75. If the price of wheat on the world market went above the ceiling prices of $5 in the case of Red Spring and $7.50 in the case of Durum, and it did so on several occasions, the producer of the grain was then subsidizing the consumers of Canada for the difference between the ceiling price and the actual world market price.
Up to the end of 1978 this producer subsidy amounted t some $35 million. If you examine the records, you will find fo the first four months of the 1979-80 crop year the wheat producers' subsidy to the consumers of Canada was some $22 million. Since January 1 the subsidy by the western grain producers to the consumers in Canada has been approximately $1 million per week.
We have only two products in Canada which come under a two-price system and both of these products come from western Canada. They are wheat and oil. There is nothing moving into western Canada, either from central Canada or other parts of Canada, at less than the market price. Over the years, western Canadians have subsidized the consumers of oil to the tune of approximately $20 billion. In the case of wheat, the western grain producers have subsidized the consumers of Canada in the last six or seven years to the tune of about $80 million. Is there any wonder that there is a feeling of alienation in the west and a strong feeling of separatism? This feeling is not just on the part of fringe groups or radicals. As I travel through my constituency I find that many responsible and respected people raise this issue with me. They mention that perhaps westerners would be better off if they went it alone. So it can be seen that the seeds of separatism have been sown and they cannot be ignored.
I said earlier in quoting the Hon. Otto Lang, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board when he submitted this bill for second reading, that the bill was for a period of seven years. The New Democratic Party supported the government in this regard. At that time this party, the official opposition, submitted an amendment to have the bill run only until 1977 rather than 1980. It was the Hon. Jack Horner, who was then on this side of the House, who submitted that amendment. I would like to read one paragraph of what he said when he submitted the amendment. This is recorded at page 5538 of the May 6, 1975, edition of Hansard, as follows:
July 7, 1980

This bill locks the wheat producer into a seven-year agreement. I cannot overemphasize that. Everyone in this House has witnessed several labour negotiations. 1 can recite the railway negotiations, the longshoremen on the west coast, grain handlers and longshoremen on the St. Lawrence, and so on. None of them relate to a seven-year contract.
He concluded by saying:
What has this Parliament got against wheat producers? Why lock them into a fixed price for their commodity?
As I said, he proposed an amendment to reduce the term by three years. And, as I said, the New Democratic Party were quick to point out that it was kind of nice to lock the farmers in for seven years, but they find now that the government, for some reason or another, did decide to terminate the subsidy in 1978. The seven-year period under the bill would run out July 31, 1980.
The problem is that the grain producers of western Canada under that bill carried out their part of the bargain. It was the government in the fall of 1978 which decided to terminate the subsidy payment to the consumers. As of November 30, 1978, the government ceased to make any further payments under the bill. The government did not come to Parliament and tell members that things were tough; that the government was going on an austerity program; that the two-price system was costing about $100 million a year and that the treasury just could not afford it. The government did not suggest that we review the program to see what we could do about it. Alternatively, the government could easily have complied with subsection 3 of section 5 of the Two-Price Wheat Act which reads as follows:
The minister shall, on an annual basis and in consultation with the producers, review the provisions of this act and all related regulations enacted by the governor in council with a view to making such recommendations to the governor in council as are appropriate in the light of prevailing costs of production of wheat and returns to producers.
The government did neither of these things. In the arrogant and high-handed manner which has characterized the Liberal government for so many years, it arbitrarily discontinued paying the subsidy. It broke the law in the same manner as you and I might break the law if we refused to pay our income tax, or if the wheat producers in western Canada delivered grain to other than the Canadian Wheat Board. If we had done that, we would have been punished; the producer would have been punished. He would have been fined, and possibly he would have been sent to jail.
But what does the government do? The government says that it is above the law. It says that about $200 million is owed and we are legally bound to pay it. We could be sued, but really there is no problem. We will simply pass a bill with retroactive effect which says that, despite the fact the two-price system was to be in effect for a period of seven years until 1980, the program came to an end on November 30, 1978, the day when the government decided that it would no longer make any payments under the act.
This is what the bill is all about, Mr. Speaker. We are asked to pass on a bill which, under section 3, says:
This act shall be deemed to have come into force on December 1, 1978.
Two-Price Wheat Act
We are here tonight debating a bill submitted by the government which it says is "deemed to have come into force on December 1, 1978." This is some one and a half years ago. We are being asked to make legal the illegal acts of this Liberal government and to wipe the record clean, in other words give it an unconditional discharge.
But, Mr. Speaker, though we are repealing the bill tonight this is not an end of the two-price system, as my hon. friend from Kindersley-Lioydminster said. The two-price system has simply been taken out of the hands of Parliament and placed into the hands of the Canadian Wheat Board which can fix the price by regulation-as a matter of fact, they have done so. On May 26 of this year Senator Hazen Argue, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board, announced the terms of Canada's new two-price system for wheat. He said this:
The new minimum and maximum prices for Canadian wheat sold for domestic human consumption will be five dollars and seven dollars per bushel, basis No. 1 Canada Red Spring at Thunder Bay.
He said further:
Effective August I the new Durum floor price for domestic consumption will be five dollars per bushel.
Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that this new pricing by the Canadian Wheat Board was arbitrary and was made without consultation and without discussion with the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory Committee. It is interesting to see that these increases in prices are effective as of August 1, because in the meantime the western grain producer is losing approximately $1 million per week. This is cash out of the producers' pockets and it is a direct subsidy to the consumers of Canada. It is also interesting to note that when the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) was minister of transport and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board he had arranged with cabinet and Treasury Board to increase the price for domestic wheat for human consumption which would have put one million dollars more per week into the hands of the western grain producers. The present government was not prepared to carry out that commitment but has been prepared to say, "Let the western grain producer subsidize the consumers of Canada to the tune of a million dollars per week until August 1."
During the debate on the bill, back in 1974, the member for Vegreville, as he then was, made this comment, as reported at page 865 of Hansard of October 29, 1974:
This bill lacks an effective measure to take into consideration the increased costs of production. Therefore we would recommend to the minister the implementation of such a provision to reflect the rising costs of production over the seven-year period.
From 1973 to 1979, including the second quarter, the costs of total farm inputs had increased by some 80.6 per cent. The index of crop production expenses, taking into consideration such items as seed and fertilizer and pesticides, had increased by some 105.5 per cent. The cost of agricultural chemicals alone had increased by 168 per cent. Mr. Speaker, had there been a mechanism in the bill to deal with increased costs of production, and had there been an annual review as provided

for in subsection 3 of section 5 of the act, the government would never had found itself in the position it is today, namely, presenting a bill to legalize its illegal acts.
Then again, this government has always shown and still shows a callous disregard for the west and, in particular, for the western grain producer. One has only to look back over the past few months and consider the uncertainty which has surrounded the port of Prince Rupert; one has only to look at the statements by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) who has cast doubt on the future of a number of railway branch lines which had been placed in the basic network by the party on this side of the Elouse when it was in power.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to participate for a while in this debate. Agriculture is important. Wheat is very important, one of the most important commodities produced in this country, if not the most important one. The bill before us this evening will extend the two-price system for wheat in this country. What a two-price system means is one price for the wheat we consume as human beings domestically in our country, and another price for wheat sold internationally. We have had that kind of system for our grain since 1973. Under the old act, as hon. members have already said tonight, it was to go on for seven years, until 1980. So we are really debating a very interesting piece of legislation.
First of all we are debating a piece of legislation which originated in the Senate. 1 want to just say a word here. I believe the bill should be rewritten in this place, in the House of Commons where members are elected democratically, where members are responsible to their constituents on a democratic basis, not in the Senate, a place to which people are appointed.
The bill before us today is really going to legalize the ending of a subsidy on November 30, 1978, for bread for consumers in our country. The subsidy was brought to an end by an order in council, by cabinet. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board was not there then, but the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was, back in 1978, and they dropped the subsidy which was worth several million dollars a year to ordinary Canadians from coast to coast. They dropped it without consultation in Parliament, without consulting those affected, low-income groups and others, and we are really
being asked tonight to legalize the action of the government back in November, 1978.
The other thing about the bill is that it increases the floor price to farmers for grain for domestic consumption. I obviously agree with that aspect. But let us take a look at why this issue is so important to us. First, as I mentioned, wheat is very important to the prairies and to the country. It is the most important commodity we have. Indeed, we are a tremendously large exporter of wheat, second in the world in terms of exports. It is worth a lot of money in terms of foreign exchange, our trade, jobs, and employing farmers on the prairies. There is not much we as a nation can do about grain we sell internationally, but there is something we can do about grain that is sold domestically.
What this bill does is increase the floor from $3.25 to $5 a bushel, but it puts a ceiling of $7 a bushel in the place of a ceiling of $5 a bushel, and I am somewhat concerned about that ceiling. As one hon. member said today, wheat now at Vancouver is selling for $6.73 a bushel. That is already very close indeed to the ceiling. If the price of wheat keeps going up the rate it has been going up for the last year or so, it will break through the ceiling very shortly, and we will have farmers again subsidizing consumers for bread and grain we, as human beings, use. So what I suggest to the government and to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), is that he consider changing the formula of the two-price wheat system and instead base it on the cost of production so that, if the cost of production goes up, the farmer will receive an increase in the price of wheat sold in this country. If the cost of production goes down, which is unlikely, then the price would go down.
I have here a brief from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture written a few weeks ago in which the federation suggested this type of system. Based on that system the price would be $5.40 for a bushel of grain, and each year there would be an annual adjustment based on a Statistics Canada report, namely, the farm input price index. The price index went up by 11 per cent last year, and therefore the price should be adjusted by an upward push of some 11 per cent. The principal suggestion I want to make to the government tonight is that the government consider changing the two-price wheat system and base it on a cost of production formula. If we did that, the farmer would not be subsidizing the consumer.
Up until 1978 the farmer subsidized the consumer by $35 million. I think it was the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) who said that in 1979 the subsidy was $22 million, and now it is an extra $1 million a week. I think that is very unfair. We should not have one sector of society subsidizing the whole society, particularly when that sector is barely getting a price which meets its cost of production, let alone providing a decent salary for grain producers.
If we look at the cost input for grain, any study which has been undertaken shows that the farmer is barely breaking even. The price of grain is not excessively high. It has not been
July 7, 1980

set by some oil sheik in Saudi Arabia or Kuwait. The price of grain is not excessively high. Therefore for the grain we sell in our own country and for our own use, the farmer should not be subsidizing the consumer, and this is one way of getting around it.
The other thing I wanted to say is that 1 think the government should be putting a great deal of time and effort into trying to reach an international grains agreement or an international commodity agreement based on the same philosophy we use for the two-price wheat system. There should be a minimum price so that the producer is getting back the cost of production plus a decent salary, and a maximum price so that the consumer on the other side is not being shafted. I think that should be the objective for all commodities in the world. I think people in the world should get together and hammer out an agreement. They should take into consideration the cost of production and salaries for producers, whether they be producers of grain, copper, bananas, tobacco or whatever commodities.
A minimum-maximum price should be set, and there should be a sliding scale where there is a cost of production formula built in. Perhaps that is an ideal. Perhaps I am being an idealist by suggesting something like that, but 1 think Canada is a nation which is immensely respected in the world, and it could lead the way in trying to persuade other peoples to try to have international commodity agreements worked out between consumers and producers. There is a big difference between this and OPEC. OPEC is an organization strictly of producers. It is an organization of petroleum exporters, and it has set up a cartel. The producers, and the producers only, determine what the price to consumers should be. I am arguing tonight that consumers and producers should get together to determine a fair price for consumers and producers. There should be harmony in the marketplace. Then, for goodness sake, let us take these commodities out of the hands of international speculators. Let us take them from the futures market, where prices bob up and down like yo-yos or dice at a casino.
All we have to do is look at the price of sugar today. The price has gone up 200 per cent or 300 per cent in the last few months, and most of the reason for that is speculation. People like to play the futures market and make a few bucks. They buy sugar stocks. There has been a cutback in the supply of sugar in the world. There have been crop failures. There is not a real shortage; it is just that supplies are being restricted a bit. There is still enough in storage to supply the world market, but because of a cutback in supply and because of weather, the commodity market has gone a little wild. Speculators have been driving up the price. Who is going to pay? The ordinary consumers who have to go out and buy the commodity. We should have as an objective taking these commodities off the futures market and off the stock market and putting the control of prices into the hands of peoples so that we have an international agreement based on the real factors and not on something which is very artificial.

I cannot hear the minister, but perhaps in his remarks later on he can respond to some of these suggestions which are being made. Since from time to time he likes to think of himself as a progressive liberal I am sure that he will be moving in this direction.
The other thing which I think is important to look at is the fact that when the price of wheat goes up, the price of bread always goes up faster. The wheat component of a loaf of bread is only 11 per cent. The wheat component accounts for only 11.5 cents of a 24-ounce loaf of bread. However, under this act when the wheat component went up by some 1.25 cents per loaf and the price of a loaf was raised by three cents by some companies and two cents by others, the federal government had no way of stopping that. The federal government has not set up a fair prices commission which could go to a company telling it that the cost of its raw material has not gone up by any more than 1.25 cents per loaf yet the price of bread has gone up by two cents or three cents a loaf, and the company involved could be forced to roll back the price. I think that is something we should be doing.
The other thing is that the subsidy which was dropped by the government in 1978 should not have been dropped at all. I was saying earlier this evening that I think it is wrong for farmers to subsidize consumers for the price of their commodity when they are barely breaking even. At the same time I want to make it very clear that I think we should have a food policy so that some of the basic foods such as bread and milk are subsidized for ordinary people. We used to have a bread subsidy and a milk subsidy. When we look at the health standards of Canadians, we find that many people are undernourished. Perhaps they are overfed, but they are undernourished, and many people are not receiving enough of the basic foods. 1 think the government should be spending a few tens of millions of dollars every year subsidizing basic foods such as whole wheat bread and milk. I think we would be saving a lot of money when it comes to bills for medicare and hospitalization on the other side.
I think it was the Food Prices Review Board which said a number of years ago that about 40 per cent of our hospital days are tied in some way to the diets of Canadians. If we could save just a miniscule percentage of that through better nutrition and a food policy, we would indeed be making a real contribution to Canadian health and to our economy.
When 1 talk about the fact that the farmer should not be subsidizing the consumer, I am not saying that the consumer should be paying a higher price for some of these basic nutritious foods which are the basics of life. What I am saying is that our society as a whole should be making a commitment to make sure that the young people and all of the people of this country have basic and decent diets.
One could give many statistics about deficiencies amongst the Canadian people. One that struck me was that 70 per cent of old age pensioners in Canada suffer from calcium deficiency, when we have a capacity in this country to produce so much milk.

July 7, 1980
Two-Price Wheat Act
Another point I want to make before concluding is that the government, by doing what it has done with the two-price system, by establishing such a low ceiling, by making sure that farmers have to subsidize consumers over the years, is increasingly encouraging a feeling of hostility on the prairies toward the central government, toward the federal government of this land. Many Liberals wonder why they have not done better in the west. This is one of the many reasons why their party has not done better. There is a real feeling that the federal government does not understand us, and if it does understand us, that it does not really care about giving us a fair deal. If it is not just the two-price system on wheat, it is the lack of adequate assistance on the drought. A farmer told me the other day, "The federal government is giving us $60 million, but they gave Chrysler, one company, some $200 million". We are not complaining about aid to Chrysler, but there should be more equity and fairness.
There is the boycott of grain to the Soviet Union. Who is that going to hurt? I should like to refer the Minister of Transport to what is happening in the United States. Even Ronald Reagan said, "If you elect me president, we will terminate the boycott of grain to the Soviet Union". One reason he would do it, and one reason we should terminate this boycott, is that the boycott is not working. Time magazine said three or four weeks ago that the Americans are shipping as much grain now through the back door to the Soviet Union as they shipped through the front door in the last few years, that big companies like Cargill and Continental Grain are using third countries to transship grain on the way to the Soviet Union. They are finding other ways of getting their grain to Soviet Russia.
The only people who are suffering, in my opinion, are the farmers of Canada because of the fact that the grain companies are shipping their grain, because of the fact that the Soviet Union is going to other countries which ship grain to them and increasing their orders, countries such as Argentina. Therefore the farmers are suffering and the grain boycott is not having any effect on the situation in Afghanistan or on Mr. Brezhnev in the Soviet Union. If it is having any impact at all, it is creating some shortage of cattle and livestock in the Soviet Union, and if it is having any effect, the effect is on the poor people, not on leaders, and, of course, on the Canadian farmers.
I appeal to the government tonight to think about grain farmers, to terminate the boycott and start the shipping of grain to the Soviet Union because, if we do not, other people will do it.
These are some of the issues about which I am concerned in the bill before us today. A number of suggestions have already been made to the House by members of the Conservative party, and one does not have to repeat them. I just want to say in closing that I hope the government will change its policy when it comes to the two-price wheat system, that it will base the price of domestic grain for human consumption, grain we buy to feed ourselves-I want to say to the House that it is the
minority of the grain we produce-on a cost of production formula so that the farmers will be paid for the minority of their grain according to the cost of producing it. In other words, it will be a cost of production index such as there is on MPs' salaries, in the cost of living increase, in the salaries of many unionized workers, and in the price of most commodities we buy where the wholesale and retail prices go up. Let us do the same for the farmers as we are doing for the other people in this country. If we do that, the farmers of this country will be much happier and much more productive, and they will produce an even greater amount of food for the people of Canada and for the people of an increasingly hungry world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) responsible for the Wheat Board is in the House during this debate. He has been in the House on several other occasions when this debate went forward, and it is an extremely important debate, as I am sure he will agree. Yet he has remained strangely silent throughout the debate up to the present moment. No doubt he is absorbing and listening to all the advice that has been given during the course of discussion and is becoming increasingly aware of the fact that the grain farmers on the prairies are in a critical situation. We hope that one of these days he will rise to his feet with some positive answers to many of the worth-while suggestions that have been made during the course of the debate.
Not only has the minister been listening carefully to the debate but he made a pilgrimage to Manitoba this week. We had an invasion in Manitoba over the weekend, and 1 had the opportunity of travelling west on the plane on Friday morning and meeting some of my colleagues from the government side of the House and pointing out to them that it was bad enough that we had drought on the prairies but now we were suffering from an invasion of locusts. Locusts devour everything before them as they go. I say that as a preliminary to a few comments I wish to make on this important subject, and I hope that in the words which I shall speak here tonight I will be able to convey to the responsible minister and to the government the growing urgency of the cost-price squeeze suffered by the grain producers on the prairies.
Unfortunately, this is not the first time that the Liberal government has taken the attitude which is represented in the bill which was first put forward in 1974, and again is being put forward in the legislation before the House. As a matter of fact I am here as a member of Parliament because of the same attitude of the Liberal government-and we have had many Liberal governments down through the years-toward the pricing position of prairie producers way back in the 1940s and 1950s.
During the war years the prairie producers, as an act of patriotism, agreed to a price under the British wheat agreement which would subsidize the consumers, the people of the United Kingdom who were largely bearing the brunt of World War II and enduring most of the suffering. The prairie farmers, who have always been outstanding Canadians, have always produced food for the world market at a price which,
July 7, 1980

most times, was lower than the cost of production. They agreed to a special pricing under the British wheat agreement, never anticipating that, following the war, they would have to bear the full brunt of this subsidization.
I remember fighting my first election on the strength of the British wheat agreement and the failure of the then Liberal government to come forward with any substantial part of the subsidy, the whole burden of which had been borne by the producers in that far off period. My opponent was mooted to become the minister of agriculture replacing the then well-known Hon. James G. Gardiner. I am referring to the Hon. Grant MacEwan who went on to fame and fortune in other vineyards, mostly in the province of Alberta. I can remember Mr. MacEwan who was then the dean of agriculture for the University of Manitoba promising that there would be a substantial contribution by the then Liberal government to subsidize prairie farmers who, over a long period of time, had sold their product at reduced prices. So, what we are seeing among latter day Liberals is a repetition of the same attitude toward prairie producers. Obviously they have forgotten nothing and learned nothing since that time.
The last election was precipitated unceremoniously, the second election in less than six months. Instead of allowing the new Conservative government to get on with the business of the nation which it was doing in quite progressive terms, the Liberal party was surprised when it was practically wiped out on the prairies. 1 submit it was inevitable this should happen because of its long continuing attitude which showed a complete lack of sensitivity and a complete unawareness of the longstanding problems of prairie grain producers. As far as I can see, at the conference in Winnipeg last weekend there was really no attempt to come to grips with these problems which have reduced the Liberal party to the unfortunate position where it speaks for only one part of Canada and is almost without a voice in the four western provinces.
1 hear the minister muttering from his front bench, and he is smiling. I hope he will rise to his feet and in firm tones tell us that the Liberal party has had a change of heart and that by listening to the words of wisdom on this side of the House, and particularly in communing with the grass roots in Winnipeg last weekend, it now realizes that there are fundamental changes which must be made on the part of the government in its attitude toward western Canada.
I do not want to be repetitive in this debate, but 1 want to point out that even the former minister, the Hon. Otto Lang, was aware of what he was doing when he carried this legislation through the House in 1974. 1 have the quotation before me which indicates that he said it was a subsidy for consumers and that it had nothing to do with subsidizing the producers. I shall deal with this in a moment, but quite firm promises were made by the then minister to overcome some of the criticisms made at that time during a rather lengthy debate. Instead of coming up with answers, the Liberal government in 1978 unceremoniously cancelled the subsidy. It did not stick to its
Two-Price Wheat Act
basic agreement which indicated that the subsidy would carry through until the end of the current crop year.
As my colleagues on this side of the House have said, this legislation is trying to legalize the termination date. November 30, 1978, was the date when the subsidy was cancelled, rather than allowing it to continue to the end of July, 1980, which was in the original program provided by the 1974 legislation. This act will not be proclaimed until the commencement of the new crop year on August 1. It means that prairie grain farmers will have to write off one whole crop year at a time of growing financial strain.
I want to point out a few suggestions whereby the minister responsible for the Wheat Board can make changes in the legislation which hopefully will do away with or deal with some of the criticisms which have been made on this side of the House. Of course the basic criticism is that it does nothing to deal with the rising costs to producers. Perhaps I should put on the record just how astronomically these costs have risen since 1973. The cost of total farm inputs or the cost of production to farmers has increased to the extent of 80.6 per cent from 1973 to the second quarter of 1979. Yet the government removed the subsidy, froze the price over a seven-year period, and totally ignored the impossible financial strait-jacket into which farmers were being put by this astronomical inflation increase which derived mostly from the irresponsible economic and financial policies of the last Liberal government.
I should like to refer to the index of crop production expenses which includes seed, fertilizers and pesticides. The cost of those necessary ingredients in production have gone up by 105.5 per cent. The cost of fertilizer alone has gone up by 115 per cent. I should note there that the farmers have been leaving the land in droves because of the impossible financial position in which they find themselves. Survivors would never have been able to keep up with the increasing demand for grain and grain products had it not been for the increasing use of fertilizers on vast prairie grain areas. Their price has increased by 115 per cent. Agricultural chemicals have gone up by 168 per cent. So, I am sure one can understand from those few statistics why 10,000 farmers a year have left the agricultural industry on the prairies. Now the situation has reached the crisis point because of the problem of drought, the rising costs of capital, and the failure of the government to deal with transportation of the increased production of crops over recent years.
Let me refer to some meetings I held recently with my own producers. The Brandon-Souris constituency is one of the richest agricultural grain producing areas of western Canada. In fact the city of Brandon is still known as the "Wheat City" of the west. I have had meetings with farmers who, I thought, would be in a very strong financial position. These meetings have been attended by farmers and their families, many of whom go into second and third generation farm people, and they have sounded a note of panic, suggesting that not only will they be leaving the agricultural industry, but that they will be leaving because of impending bankruptcy. The reason for the impending bankruptcy I think should be obvious after the

July 7, 1980
Two-Price Wheat Act
statistics I have quoted. One cannot continue to sell a product at well below the cost of production, and hope to survive.
The statistics I just presented to the House will, I am sure, demonstrate that this has been a losing game and has now become critical because these farmers who have survived by reason of hard work, by extending their holdings in order to become more productive, by fertilizing, using insecticides, mechanizing, with all the other ingredients that go into the production of grain today, are now facing the prospect of very little production this year. The present estimate is that they will receive about 50 per cent or less than the normal level, with no income to survive the economic crunch in which they find themselves. This is now an emergency situation.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was in the House earlier. He travelled all the way to Yorkton the other day to announce there was a drought emergency. He was addressing mainly members of the cattle industry, and he announced policies to convince the dairy farmer and cattle producer not to destroy their basic herds in order to keep their heads above the overwhelming economic waters. These policies do nothing to solve the problem of the grain producer. The grain producer is the individual caught in the cost-price squeeze, and the one in some cases, particularly in my constituency and in other areas of western Canada, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, who is faced with crop failure. The Minister of Agriculture realized there must be an infusion of cash to the tune of $60 million.
On the other hand the Minister of Transport in this case is depriving grain producers of $200 million which would have been made available under the subsidy had it not been arbitrarily cancelled on November 30, 1978.

of decision as he has listened to the debate-let me say that I hope that he will introduce some flexibility into the legislation. It is not fair to freeze farm prices for a period of seven years. When agreements are made with labour unions they sometimes last only one year. This happened with the Canadian Union of Postal Workers recently, which received a fairly generous agreement compared to what the legislation before us is providing to the basic grain producers of Canada, who produce a product which is urgently needed. As I have already indicated, these farmers are facing a crisis which is not of their own making, and because of the problem of drought many of our best producers will go out of business.
There should be continuing negotiation for a world price on wheat. It has been said before, but it bears repetition: there was a time when the price of a bushel of wheat as it was related to a barrel of oil cost about $2.50. Both of these resources are basic to the Canadian economy and to the world economy. It is the western producers who are feeling the brunt in this country. I look directly at the minister and I say that that is why his party has no support in western Canada, because they do not even grasp the problem. That is why I hope he will make a statement before we proceed much further in this debate. The farmers cannot continue to sell their grain below the cost of production. There must be some adjustment for the inflation which has eroded the value of the dollar since 1973 by more than 50 per cent.
We must stop the exodus of the basic producer away from the land, which is occurring at a rate of 10,000 per year. I am sure that the exodus will increase by much more than that figure because of the impending bankruptcies due to the high cost of credit and capital, as farmers try to expand their holdings and their producing capacity. I trust that both the Minister of Agriculture, who has made some initial attempts, and the Minister of Transport, who is responsible for the Wheat Board, will either withdraw this act and pay the $200 million which is owed to the western grain producers, or bring in a revised act which does not freeze prices unrealistically for seven years, which is flexible and meets the costs of production and which will protect our grain producers in a drastic time of economic crisis.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill S-6, an act to amend the Two-Price Wheat Act. I would like to speak from the point of view of Canadian consumers. In so doing I must say that I am very proud to be joining the protest which was first raised in 1978 by many consumers and senior citizens groups across Canada, groups who were very concerned because the Liberal government of the day was removing subsidies on bread and pasta.
In these earlier protests it was predicted the price of bread would soar, and it has. The price of pasta has increased by 25 per cent. The prices of both items have increased far beyond the value of the subsidy. This, of course, is as the result of the direct withdrawal of the government subsidy. Bill S-6 will
Two-Price Wheat Act
finally remove all government responsibility for subsidizing the present exorbitant cost of bread.
I think it is particularly symbolic of this government that bread, the staff of life, is the topic of this retrogressive bill and that it reflects the values and attitudes of it toward the needs of ordinary Canadians, particularly the needs of the over one million poor people in Canada today. As we know, bread is the staple food for most Canadians, with rice and pasta the alternatives in some ethnic groups. Bread is an essential food item for low income families on welfare who cannot afford to buy fresh produce or fresh meats more than once or twice a month. It is also very essential to the livelihood of our western wheat farmers.
Despite these facts, as my colleague and other colleagues have mentioned, in September, 1978, the skim milk subsidy program was dropped by the Liberal government, followed by the termination of bread subsidies in December. The Conservatives, I believe, supported these cutbacks. These subsidies were removed at the very same time that inflation was on the rise. We know that soaring food costs were putting great stress on family budgets such as they are today.
We in the New Democratic Party oppose this bill just as strongly as we opposed the cutbacks in 1978. With the high price of food today, the budgets and meals of low income families are affected, and I am sure that most families are shocked after their weekly shopping trips. For example, the magazine Ottawa Today conducted a survey of local food prices which showed that eggs are up to $1.19 a dozen, bread costs 65 cents a loaf, frozen fish costs $2.39, apples cost 98 cents per pounds, and milk costs 72 cents a quart. If one compares these prices with the prices in my riding of Vancouver East, they will find that prices there are even higher. In British Columbia the cost of a loaf of bread is now close to 99 cents. It is quite significant of our lack of Canadian policy when we know that people in British Columbia can go across the border to Seattle and pick up three loaves of breads for $1, which is the price the people of British Columbia pay for one loaf.
We also know that it is cheaper and easier for children to go into a store and buy a chocolate bar or a package of potato chips than it is to purchase a delicious Canadian apple. Local cherries in season in Vancouver cost about $1 a pound and a package of five beets costs 59 cents at the height of the season. There is no question in my mind that this supports the NDP position that there must be a fair prices review board with power to roll back prices and to take a good look at profit, particularly those of the supermarkets.
The high cost of food is not a trivial matter. It certainly relates to the bill which is before us tonight. It is an established scientific fact, and hon. members can refer to the recent report which was put out by the Year of the Child Commission, that children who are born of pregnant mothers who do not have proper nourishment suffer from irreparable brain damage, and many of these are poor children. They start life with damaged brains which will make it impossible for them to be fully mature people in society.

July 7, 1980
Two-Price Wheat Act
It is also well established, and I have had experience with this myself, that pre-school children who do not have the proper nutritious diet suffer from poor co-ordination, lethargy, and inadequate physical, intellectual and social development. It is no wonder that when these same youngsters get to elementary school they are the underachievers, the people who are categorized as having learning disabilities and behavioural problems, and who are the problem makers as they grow toward adolescence. Pretty soon they become the troublemakers, as they reach adolescence.
We can take responsibility for a good part of these social and personal problems because there is a very direct link between inadequate nutrition, poor diet, and the lack of development that we see in many of these children. Often their parents cannot afford proper food and are themselves poorly nourished and apathetic. The whole relationship of inadequate diet and food is an important part of the syndrome of poverty.
This bill has particular significance for millions of poor people in Canada. It should be opposed for the same reasons that many senior citizens on limited incomes protested against the termination of food subsidies in 1978.
I should like to remind hon. members of a few further facts about poverty. Families on social assistance have very little money available for food. Neither do they have money for transportation to go and hunt for bargains in food or to go to the hinterlands to buy directly from the farmers. They cannot afford to buy freezers and take advantage of bulk purchase prices. Although they have the least amount of money in their food budgets of any people, they have to pay the highest prices. Usually the only place they can shop for a few items at a time is the corner grocery store. By the end of the month these families are eating spaghetti, bread, or sandwiches without meat.
In British Columbia a family of four on social assistance receives $334 per month. That does not include shelter. Out of this they must buy bus tickets, clothing, school supplies, recreation, if they have any, as well as food. We know now that nutritionists say it requires well over $300 per month at today's prices to provide a nutritious and adequate diet for a growing family of four people.
If you were living alone, Mr. Speaker, even with parliamentary dining room privileges, I doubt if you could feed yourself on $136 per month. This is what a single person on welfare receives today and it must cover all expenses, including food. 1 wonder how such people can possibly afford to buy bread which is now close to $1 per loaf.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR HEARINGS ON ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL POTATO MARKETING AGENCY
AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR HEARINGS ON ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL POTATO MARKETING AGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 16 I put the following question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), and I quote:
In view of the apparent general support among potato growers for the concept of a national potato marketing agency, will the minister ask the Farm Products Marketing Council to initiate public hearings this summer in order to move toward that objective; and if they will not do that, will the minister immediately
Adjournment Debate
establish a commission of inquiry, on an urgent basis, to look into the potato industry in Canada?
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture replied saying that indeed he had been in touch with the National Farm Products Marketing Council and had asked it to hold public hearings to inquire into the potato industry. He added, and 1 quote:
1 believe I can safely say that hearings will be held this summer on the proposals, especially by the provinces of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, that a regional agency be established for the eastern production region of Canada, including Ontario, Quebec, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
Since then, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture-if I am to believe an article I read in the newspaper Le Droit of Ottawa on last Thursday or Friday which I unfortunately do not have with me at this time, the Minister of Agriculture came back charging and said he hoped the Farm Products Marketing Council would undertake as soon as possible to hold public hearings with a view to eventually establishing that potato marketing board that all or nearly all people are now calling for forcefully, of course, because of the poor situation in which the potato industry has been for the past three years, without going back further.
The other aspect of my question, Mr. Speaker, consisted in asking the minister whether the Farm Products Marketing Council did not want to go ahead immediately and hold public hearings with a view to establishing a potato marketing board.
1 asked the minister whether he was prepared to set up an independent commission of inquiry into all aspects of the potato industry. I think there is no point in reminding the many hon. members listening to me tonight and the Minister of Agriculture that during the few months we were in the opposition 1 advocated the establishment of that independent commission of inquiry to report as soon as possible. And, fortunately, that proposal did not die on the shelves as the Liberal party in its great wisdom decided to include it in its agricultural platform. And I remember full well, among other things, a large page of advertising that was published in a farming weekly in the province of Ontario which was paid for by the Liberal party and where one could see the picture of the present Minister of Agriculture, who is still the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Whelan, containing that election commitment to establish as soon as possible an independent commission of inquiry into all aspects of the potato industry in Canada and to have it report to the government on an urgent basis.
Mr. Speaker, I know that the Minister of Agriculture has only the best of intentions when he urges the officials of the Farm Products Marketing Agency to hold public hearings as soon as possible. However, this is only one part of a much more complex problem, and as evidence I would like to quote a
2632

Adjournment Debate
letter dated January 7 that I received from one of the big names in the potato industry, McCain Foods Limited:

Obviously, it would not matter to us one way or the other if an inquiry was held. I am certainly not opposed to it.
The problems of the potato industry are not simple. I don't think it is any one item that is giving us troubles-it is probably a series.

I could also quote many letters that I received at my office from simple farmers, people who deal solely with the production of potatoes and who support what I have said to the effect that it is urgent to get to the bottom of this situation, because when an industry like the potato industry has marked ups and downs for about 15 years, we have to wonder not if the industry is sick, but rather what stage of its agony it has reached, because, in my opinion, the potato industry is more than sick, it is agonizing.
When 1 speak about the potato industry, 1 have the impression that 1 know what I am talking about, and 1 am thinking mostly about the independent producers, the small family farms with 100, 150 or 200 acres and other family operations which might farm well over 500 acres.
However, I am thinking mostly about these hundreds of average producers for whom the state of the markets, the state of all the marketing structures and the government policies at the federal and provincial levels have become matters of life and death. No one in this industry and no one at the federal level is able now to pinpoint the trouble. 1 am not more of an expert than others, but I am ready to admit that, as written in the letter that 1 quoted earlier, we have a whole series of problems and that the simple fact of establishing a potato marketing agency will not get to the bottom of the situation and bring the potato industry back to health or to life. I therefore look forward to hearing the comments of the Minister of Agriculture because in the past, he has always responded very humanely to the problems which affect the various sectors of agricultural production in Canada.
