Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member 1 will repeat a little of what I have already said. On May 29 I directed the National Farm Products Marketing Council to inquire into the merits of forming a marketing agency under the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act and report the findings to me with dispatch.
Some people may have different ideas as to what "dispatch" means, but according to the act it means that after public notification has been given, hearings can be held within 45 days. They have held meetings with all the provinces they felt were interested and which have experienced this economic drought because they were producing a product-but they were as badly off as the farmers in western Canada who have nothing to sell; these people produce the product but they could not sell it, and in many instances a lot of it came to
July 7, 1980
destruction through deterioration since there was no market for it. What we are saying to these producers is: let us organize properly so as to get rid of the kind of economic drought you face four years out of five, as the record will show.
There has been very little co-operation between the provinces which are the main producing provinces in Canada. That has to be a fact. Or else we can do as an old Conservative government did under R. B. Bennett when he forced a Canadian Wheat Board on the west in 1935-we could force a Canadian potato marketing commission on potato producers. That may be the only answer to getting a proper marketing system for the product because of the great inequity there is in the potato business.
We are also receiving messages from provinces like British Columbia and Alberta, saying, "Please do not leave us out of any marketing commission or agency that you are going to set up for potatoes because we want to be in it." We are receiving that kind of representation. 1 had further discussions late last week with the National Farm Products Marketing Council. The council is prepared to go ahead because now the provinces of Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario have said they want a tough agency. They want those kinds of hearings to be held with regard to the marketing of potatoes in eastern Canada.
So, we are on the way, but we also may be holding hearings in some of the provinces in western Canada to see whether we should go even further, because there is that authority vested in the Minister of Agriculture in the national farm products marketing legislation. I say that this is something which is long overdue. I think that a commission would only find most of the things we know already. There are many, many, bad, bad marketing practices, and the only thought I have is that if we appointed a commission it might say, "Mr. Minister, go ahead and recommend to your government that you impose a potato marketing commission or board on the producers of that product," because there is much unfairness, inequity and economic disparity existing among producers who produce a highly nutritious product but receive no returns. Many of these producers are going bankrupt. They are productive people. Something must be done, and I agree with the hon. member that something probably should have been done some time before.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-EFFECT OF NEW CUSTOMS REGULATIONS ON SMALL BUSINESS
NATIONAL REVENUE-EFFECT OF NEW CUSTOMS REGULATIONS ON SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am faced with a dilemma tonight. It is now about 12 minutes after ten, and I have seven minutes to deal with a problem which I did not realize was such a monumental problem all across Canada.
On May 5 I rose to ask the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) about the use of B32 actions against small businessmen. At the time I was raising this because a constituent of mine brought to my attention the way he was being
July 7, 1980

abused by the use of this action. Subsequently I received a file about an inch thick from brokers across Canada who are bothered by this kind of action.
My dilemma is how I can talk about this subject without becoming perilously close to what sounds like civil service bashing, which 1 detest. Yet this problem has to be corrected. How can I deal with it without criticizing the people who are the cause of the problem?
After 1 raised the issue, I found that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association has addressed itself to the problem, and in one of its bulletins said:
It was stated that there was a growing tendency among port officials to adopt the attitude "Pay first and then we will listen to you" which amounts to a complete denial of the basic purpose of the 30-day grace period.
It is the customs officials who have the businessmen by the throat when they arrive at ports of entry with products they are trying to import.
Since May 5 I have found the following things. First, the practice which Revenue Canada has adopted in the customs branch may in fact be illegal. The Customs Act allows for 90 days for payment to be made on a reassessment, but the practice by the customs branch and the policy of the customs branch is to give 30 days. Is it possible for revenue policy to supersede the Customs Act? In fact the government may be facing a lawsuit on this matter. However, the customs officials know that small firms cannot afford litigation and that large firms are not bothered by the small amounts they have to pay. They can ride out that kind of storm. Small firms cannot do that, but larger firms can.
Second, I found that the practice was designed, oddly enough, to cut down on paper work. I found out through a departmental bulletin that when the B32 form was adopted, the practice took three forms to replace the one which was used previously. That is some way of cutting down on the paper burden for Canada and for the business community! The way we cut down on the paper burden in this practice is to put a pistol to the businessman's head and say, "Give me your wallet in five seconds". That is a good way of cutting down on litigation. That is a good way of cutting down the number of appeals, because if one has 30 days in this case instead of 90 days, there will be many fewer appeals. I suppose in some ways this has been effective, but it has not been fair, and that, after all, ought to be the uppermost policy of the government.
I know that customs officials cannot be expected to have on-the-spot, intricate knowledge of the multiplicity of imports arriving at the ports of entry. Let me illustrate. I have received a letter from the Minister of National Revenue dealing with this very issue. Here is what he said in this case:
The goods described as Foam Compound B, MR resins, FSC Foams Compound B, Aropol resins, and Hetron resins were also entered under tariff item 93901-1 and 93901-41, free, most favoured nation tariff rate. These have now been determined to be unsaturated polyester and polyether polyol polycondensation moulding compositions classifiable under tariff item 93901-41 at 12.5 per cent, most favoured nation tariff rate. However, it should be mentioned that when Compound A and Compound B are imported together as a system in pre-deter-
Adjournment Debate
mined mixing ratios, they are classifiable as a polyurethane polycondensation moulding composition under tariff item 93901-42 at 7.5 per cent, most favoured nation tariff rate.
I wonder if the minister understood what he was writing when he wrote that letter to me. 1 know I did not understand it when I read it. I expect that most customs officials, when an item comes to the border or many other times like it, do not understand what the item is about. If they can be human enough, as they must be, not to understand the tariff items because they are intricate, surely they can be human enough to admit when they have made a mistake. That is the bottom line of all this.
What the customs officials are doing, it seems to me, is harassing businessmen because they know that the regulations are on their side, not because they are quoting them accurately but because they are so complex that the poor businessman will have to cave in. In order to cover themselves even further, they devised B32 which means that they can go back two years and reclassify at will items which a company has imported. If you are a small manufacturer and you have imported an item two years ago, you have remanufactured it, you have sold it, you have based your price on the cost of the item plus a small margin of profit, how can you go back two years on that item which has been sold, add the extra expense to the cost and to the price and recoup your losses? It seems to me that the customs officials do not appreciate the implications of the complications that they create for the small businessman.
The minister still has not answered me how the businessman is supposed to function if the government can go back two years and the businessman has no recourse in recouping his cost. I wonder how many customs officials there are across Canada who have never had any business experience at all and therefore have never understood what happens to the businessman. In the case of my constituent it meant that the bill which was presented to him for 30 days payment wiped out the profit for two years for that company, which meant that there was no margin for error, which meant that 14 jobs were on the line, just because some official wanted a cushion of comfort to be able to go back two years.
There were three officials who reclassified those items three different ways. Could they be wrong? I expect they could be wrong. The option then is to drive these people out of business. If the government wants to do that, it can carry on with the present practice.
Let me state in conclusion that the great fear I have-and no company has said it to me-is that if a company makes a representation to a member of Parliament such as I, I wonder what will happen the next time it comes to the border. Will the customs officials harass the company even more than they have before because it had the audacity to make a representation to its member of Parliament?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-EFFECT OF NEW CUSTOMS REGULATIONS ON SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose we can only be thankful that the hon. member refrained from bashing our civil servants.

July 7, 1980
Adjournment Debate
I appreciate the opportunity the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) has given me to explain the effect of new customs regulations on small businesses. In his question of May 5 the hon. member made specific mention of the B32 assessment and the 30-day period in which payments must be made. The practice of issuing requests for additional duty and/or tax of course is not new. What is new is the requirement that such assessments be paid within 30 days. This system of payment was introduced nearly a year ago. It was done as a result of a recommendation by the financial management task force on accounting and control of revenue, refunds and drawbacks, set up because of reports and criticisms generated by international audits and by the office of the Auditor General in the areas of accounts receivable and accounts payable. As we all know, the hon. member's party is the very one which told us Liberals to pay very close attention to what the Auditor General said.
The task force recommendation was that assessments and reassessments be payable on demand. However, the system introduced was to require payment within 30 days of the date of the B32 notice. In making this recommendation, the task force observed that accounts receivable in customs were too high and there were delays in payments.
It should be noted that the Customs Act envisages the payment of duty at the time of entry of the goods and that the 30 days of grace granted in paying assessments is in accordance with current business practice. Also, the vast majority of these assessments are paid without appeal or, if appealed, the ultimate decision confirms the assessment. Of course importers have the right to appeal these assessments under the provisions of sections 46, 47 and 48 of the Customs Act. This procedure provides for an appeal eventually to the deputy minister and, if not satisfied, to the Tariff Board and the Federal Court.
The problem in accounts receivable arose as a result of a systems change in 1973-74 designed to expedite the clearance of goods at customs to the benefit of all importers. The system has been very successful in this regard. This new system permits importers or their agents to clear goods on the basis of their own declarations of duty and tax owing. In general, it is not until some time after entry, usually within four weeks, that a departmental officer reviews the entry document and first, agrees with the entry as presented; second, decides that too much duty and/or tax has been paid; or third, decides that additional duty and/or tax is owing. A B32 assessment for additional duty and/or tax may then be issued. This assessment is made on the basis of the officer's interpretation of the legislation and past departmental rulings, policy statements and instructions. Of course importers and brokers may seek guidance from departmental officers on tariff classification and valuation matters in advance of importation so as to ensure the accuracy of their declarations.
As regards the three different classification judgments on one item by three different officers, departmental officers are aware of the importance of uniformity of application of the Customs Act across the country. Substantial resources are
devoted to improving uniformity. If any situations occur when an opinion or a ruling on tariff classification will be given which conflicts with a previous opinion or ruling, the importer has recourse to the formal appeal procedure. I see Mr. Speaker is about to call my time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in connection with a question which I asked in this House on June 4 last of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) with respect to the question of rape and certain decisions which were made by the Supreme Court of Canada on this subject in recent months.
In the April 14 Speech from the Throne the Liberal government pledged that it would take strong measures to promote equality for women, saying that there was no room in Canada for sexual discrimination of any kind. One of the areas on which we were promised action was "the very serious problem of violence against women". In the meantime we have seen no sign whatsoever of the government's proposed aid to women who are victims of violence.
j
What has happened is that the Supreme Court of Canada has produced two judgments which seriously affect the laws that relate to violent crimes against women. On May 20 last the Supreme Court delivered its judgment in the case of Regina v. Pappajohn. In this judgment the court upheld the admissibility of the defence on the part of an accused that he had an honest belief the victim of the rape was consenting even though he could cite no reasonable ground for that belief.
In upholding the validity of this particular defence our Supreme Court relied upon the precedent that had earlier been set in an English case, a decision of the House of Lords in The Director of Public Prosecutions v. Morgan. In that case the House of Lords ruled that three men who were in fact convicted of rape would have been acquitted had they claimed they believed the woman they had raped at the behest of her husband was playacting when she violently resisted the assault of these three men, even though there were no reasonable grounds for that belief whatsoever. In that particular case the husband of the woman in question had said that if the three men came home and wanted to rape his wife she would put up quite a struggle, but they should ignore that because really she was just pretending. The British House of Lords held, and our Supreme Court here in Canada followed the decision, that had they honestly believed she really was just playacting they would have been acquitted completely of the charge of rape.
We see the serious effect of that in a decision which shortly followed. In the decision of Regina v. Cogan, a case in which a woman who was crying, who was protesting against the advances and the assault of a man who had been invited by her husband to rape her, in effect, the accused was acquitted. This particular man who was charged with rape was acquitted. His defence was that he thought he had the consent of the woman
July 7, 1980

because her husband had said it would be all right. That is the result of the kind of decision which our Supreme Court of Canada recently handed down in Pappajohn.
The serious implications of this decision cannot be overemphasized. The fact is that now women are going to be placed basically in the invidious position of having either to resist an attacker forcefully so it is clear beyond any doubt whatsoever they were opposing, or to submit willingly even though what that could mean is that the woman would subsequently have no recourse in law. This will, of course, mean there will be even fewer reported rapes and even fewer convictions for a crime in respect of which there is already a very low incidence of report.
On June 4 I asked the Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development what action he and his government were prepared to take to deal with the effects of this very mistaken decision on the part of our Supreme Court. I certainly hope the parliamentary secretary in the House tonight is prepared to tell the House that legislation will be forthcoming very quickly, and that it will not be included in the omnibus criminal code amendments which have been promised by the government for some time.
It is critical we recognize that these changes should redefine the nature of rape to recognize that it is not a crime of passion, but in fact is a crime of violence against women. Our law must recognize that. I certainly hope the law will also get rid of the so-called spousal immunity whereby a husband cannot be convicted of raping his wife even under the most outrageous of circumstances. This perpetrates the old myth of a woman, a wife, as a property of her husband. 1 certainly hope we will hear tonight that the government intends to remove that particular inequity in our laws in respect of sexual offences against women.
Finally I would note that, although we have seen no action whatsoever on the part of the government in this important area of violent crimes against women, we have once again in the decision of Regina v. Forsythe, by the Supreme Court of Canada, seen a very serious setback to women in the area of rape and the laws of evidence in rape trials. We have seen that our Supreme Court has permitted defence counsel now to badger and harass women about their sexual activities with other persons other than an accused, activities which are clearly and totally irrelevant to the question of whether at any given time a woman was violently or sexually assaulted by a man with a charge of rape then being laid.
We see in both the Pappajohn and in the Forsythe decisions the need for Parliament to move quickly in this area of the law, the need for long overdue amendments to protect women who have been the victims of these kinds of attacks.
In concluding, I hope that we will see, as I said earlier tonight, the review which has apparently been conducted by the department, completed, and that the crime of rape will be redefined as a crime which reflects the reality of its violent nature against women.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-EFFECT OF NEW CUSTOMS REGULATIONS ON SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the concern of the hon. member for the problems of victims of sexual assault, and 1 share those concerns with him. I do not concur with his views on the effect of the recent Pappajohn decision, to which he refers. In all seriousness I suggest that he take a closer look at the judgment before he makes and spreads abroad even more the misinterpretation of at least a part of the decision to which I will now address myself.
The Pappajohn decision of the Supreme Court of Canada affirms that what is known as a "mistake of fact" defence is available in Canada on a charge of rape. Before a judge can put a defence to the jury, there must be an evidentiary basis upon which that defence can rest. For a "mistake of fact" defence to succeed in a rape case, there must be some evidence which, if believed, would support the existence of the accused's honest but mistaken belief that the complainant was consenting to the act of sexual intercourse.
In the Pappajohn case the trial judge did not put the defence of "mistake of fact" to the jury because he was of the opinion that there was no evidentiary basis for it. The accused's defence was that the complainant consented; it was not that he mistakenly believed that the complainant consented. The majority of the judges in the Supreme Court of Canada agreed that the trial judge was correct in not putting this defence to the jury. The two dissenting judges thought that the defence should have been put to the jury.
It is incorrect to say that an accused must be acquitted even if there were no reasonable grounds for this belief. While the existence of reasonable grounds is not a pre-condition to the availability of the defence, those grounds necessarily determine the weight the jury will give to the defence.
The hon. member has also raised the matter of legislation amending the Criminal Code to deal with sexual offences against women. 1 point out to him that the code amendments under consideration right now would deal with sexual offences against men and women. I am sure that the hon. member was concerned with both instances, although his emphasis was on instances concerning women.
There was quite an extensive review over the last decade of this entire subject. As a result the government introduced Bill C-52, in the Thirtieth Parliament, which was criticized on a number of grounds, including that of redefinition of rape to indecent assault on the one hand and aggravated sexual assault in the other circumstance. Since that bill was introduced there has been a great deal of criticism from women's organizations. The Department of Justice and its officials since the introduction of that bill a couple of years ago have consulted very widely and have been assisted by the Canadian Status of Women Council in that particular respect.
I would inform the hon. member that the minister is presently reviewing all the possible alternatives on this very serious and acute subject. I am advised by the Department of Justice that the minister hopes to finalize this matter with cabinet in the coming weeks with a view to introducing a bill on the

subject as soon as possible. In the absence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) I do not wish to comment on the Forsythe decision to which the hon. member has referred. However, I want to assure him that the minister is studying that decision of the Supreme Court very carefully. Finally, I concur with the hon. member in his concern for this matter.
July 7, 1980
